    Single-frame MSSR with mssrscopR

    Source: vignettes/mssrscopR.Rmd
    mssrscopR.Rmd

    All images here are synthetic and generated in this document, so the true scene is known.

    The operator

    Mean-Shift Super-Resolution (MSSR; Torres-García et al. 2022, doi:10.1038/s41467-022-34693-9) subtracts a local, range-weighted mean-shift estimate from each pixel and refines the result over order steps. fwhm is the point-spread-function width in input pixels and has no default.

    g <- expand.grid(r = 1:31, c = 1:41)
spot <- function(r0, c0, a = 1) a * exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
pair <- function(sep) matrix(spot(16, 18) + spot(16, 18 + sep) + 0.05, 31, 41)
x <- pair(3)                       # two sources 3 px apart, FWHM 3 px
res <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
res
#> <mssr_result> intensity_weighted_structure
#>   input 31 x 41 -> output 62 x 82 (amp 2, extent grid)
#>   fwhm 3 px, order 1, kernel disk (half-size 3), mesh TRUE
#>   engine mssr_r_rev3; zero fraction 0.633
#>   Not a quantitative intensity: measure on the original data.
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(x, "input"); show(as.matrix(res), "mssr(amp = 2)")

    par(op)

    The amplified grid only adds samples. mssr_coords() places them in input-pixel units, and the field of view stays [0.5, n + 0.5]:

    range(mssr_coords(res)$col)
#> [1]  0.75 41.25
res$transform$spacing
#> row col 
#> 0.5 0.5

    How far does the separation go? Compare the value at the midpoint between the two sources with the value at a source center, in the input and in the MSSR map (values below 1 mean a dip between the sources):

    mid_ratio <- function(sep) {
  x <- pair(sep)
  r <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
  v <- as.matrix(r)
  co <- mssr_coords(r)
  row <- which.min(abs(co$row - 16))
  at_input <- function(cc) stats::approx(1:41, x[16, ], cc)$y
  at_mssr <- function(cc) stats::approx(co$col, v[row, ], cc)$y
  c(input = at_input(18 + sep / 2) / at_input(18), mssr = at_mssr(18 + sep / 2) / at_mssr(18))
}
round(rbind(`2.4 px` = mid_ratio(2.4), `2.6 px` = mid_ratio(2.6), `3 px` = mid_ratio(3)), 3)
#>        input  mssr
#> 2.4 px 1.086 1.235
#> 2.6 px 1.054 0.815
#> 3 px   0.968 0.255

    At 3 px the input shows only a shallow dip, which MSSR deepens strongly. At 2.6 px the input pixels have a single maximum, between the sources, yet MSSR returns two peaks with a clear dip (ratio below 1): it can separate sources that the pixels show merged. Its peaks move toward each other, so a ratio taken at the source centers can stay above 1 although two peaks exist. The peak positions along row 16 show this directly (true sources at 18 and 18 + separation):

    peaks <- function(sep, amp = 2) {
  r <- mssr(pair(sep), fwhm = 3, amp = amp)
  co <- mssr_coords(r)
  v <- as.matrix(r)[which.min(abs(co$row - 16)), ]
  i <- which(diff(sign(diff(v))) == -2) + 1
  co$col[i[v[i] > 0.05 * max(v)]]
}
list(`2.4 px` = peaks(2.4), `2.4 px, amp 4` = peaks(2.4, amp = 4), `2.6 px` = peaks(2.6))
#> $`2.4 px`
#> [1] 19.75
#> 
#> $`2.4 px, amp 4`
#> [1] 18.625 19.625
#> 
#> $`2.6 px`
#> [1] 18.25 20.25

    At 2.4 px MSSR returns a single, sharper peak at amp = 2; at amp = 4 it shows two peaks with a barely visible dip, 1 px apart for sources 2.4 px apart. The spacing of MSSR peaks therefore underestimates the true separation near this limit.

    Known failure modes

    MSSR is nonlinear. A dim structure next to a bright one is strongly suppressed, and broad filled objects can be hollowed or fragmented:

    y <- matrix(spot(16, 14) + spot(16, 21.5, 0.1) + 0.02, 31, 41)   # 10:1 brightness
disk <- outer(1:31, 1:41, function(r, c) as.numeric((r - 16)^2 + (c - 21)^2 <= 81))
disk <- disk + 0.02
ry <- as.matrix(mssr(y, fwhm = 3))
rd <- as.matrix(mssr(disk, fwhm = 3))
c(input_ratio = y[16, 22] / y[16, 14], mssr_ratio = ry[16, 22] / ry[16, 14],
  disk_center = rd[16, 21])
#> input_ratio  mssr_ratio disk_center 
#> 0.110379995 0.008616307 0.000000000
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(ry, "dim beside bright"); show(disk, "filled disk"); show(rd, "mssr(disk)")

    par(op)

    Extended objects are emphasized at their edges: the filled disk becomes a ring with a zero center, so segment filled objects such as nuclei on the original data. A rod three FWHM long becomes two peaks near its ends, with a lower interior:

    rod <- matrix(Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq(16.5, 25.5, length.out = 41),
                                 function(cc) spot(16, cc, 1 / 41))) + 0.002, 31, 41)
rr <- mssr(rod, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
co <- mssr_coords(rr)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(co$col, as.matrix(rr)[which.min(abs(co$row - 16)), ], type = "l",
     xlab = "column (input px)", ylab = "mssr along row 16")
lines(1:41, rod[16, ] / max(rod[16, ]) * max(rr$values), lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("mssr", "input (scaled)"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n")

    par(op)

    With noise, the mean shift also responds to noise maxima: single sources and short rods can break into several peaks, one source can look like a pair, and dim sources are lost first. An fwhm smaller than the true PSF makes false pairs more likely, and higher order values add further, mostly weak, maxima. Compare results with the input, and test settings on a synthetic noisy scene of known content that resembles your data.

    These failure modes are why the outputs are not quantitative; res$diagnostics$quantitative is always FALSE.

    Several channels or bands

    mssr() takes one 2D frame, so multichannel and spectral data are processed one channel at a time, and each channel gets its own structure map. Here channel b holds the same two sources as channel a, but its second source is half as bright; 0.5 * a is a scaled copy of a:

    a <- matrix(spot(16, 14) + spot(16, 26) + 0.05, 31, 41)
b <- matrix(spot(16, 14) + spot(16, 26, 0.5) + 0.05, 31, 41)
ra <- as.matrix(mssr(a, fwhm = 3))
rb <- as.matrix(mssr(b, fwhm = 3))
rc <- as.matrix(mssr(0.5 * a, fwhm = 3))
round(c(input = b[16, 26] / a[16, 26], mssr = rb[16, 26] / ra[16, 26],
        scaled_copy = rc[16, 26] / ra[16, 26]), 3)
#>       input        mssr scaled_copy 
#>       0.524       0.243       0.500

    The ratio of b to a at the second source falls to about half its input value, while the scaled copy keeps its ratio. A different background or another object elsewhere in one channel also changes the ratios. Ratios between channels, indices and spectra therefore belong to the original data, for example measured under a mask as below.

    Masks with measurements on the original data

    A structure map can select pixels, but measurements belong to the original image. mssr_mask() keeps an exact number of pixels of a region. tie_fraction reports the share of the selected pixels that random tie-breaking decided, and cut_relative the lowest selected score relative to the highest. The mean shift is clipped at zero, so most of this map is exactly zero; keep a share below the positive one.

    r <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3)
mean(as.matrix(r) > 0)             # share of pixels with any structure
#> [1] 0.0220299
m <- mssr_mask(r, fraction = 0.02)
c(coverage = attr(m, "coverage"), tie_fraction = attr(m, "tie_fraction"),
  cut_relative = attr(m, "cut_relative"))
#>     coverage tie_fraction cut_relative 
#>  0.020456334  0.000000000  0.002531077
c(mean_all = mean(x), mean_masked = mean(x[m]))
#>    mean_all mean_masked 
#>  0.06604718  0.58442567

    A larger share reaches into the zeros. Tie-breaking then decides most of the mask, which mssr_mask() reports with a warning:

    wide <- mssr_mask(r, fraction = 0.2)
#> Warning: The mask reaches pixels where the MSSR map shows no structure: 89% of the
#> selected pixels were chosen by tie-breaking and the lowest selected score is 0
#> of the highest. Choose a smaller `fraction` or a `region`.
attr(wide, "tie_fraction")
#> [1] 0.8901961

    Selecting pixels this way changes the measured population. It is not known to improve any downstream analysis, so evaluate it for your own task.

    Degenerate input and unsupported requests

    Flat frames return zeros flagged as degenerate. Requests the package cannot honor fail with classed errors:

    mssr(matrix(1, 5, 5), fwhm = 3)$diagnostics[c("degenerate", "degenerate_reason")]
#> $degenerate
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $degenerate_reason
#> [1] "flat input"
try(mssr(array(0, c(4, 4, 3)), fwhm = 3))     # no axis is guessed
#> Error in mssr(array(0, c(4, 4, 3)), fwhm = 3) : 
#>   `x` has 3 dimensions; process one 2D frame at a time (no axis is
#> inferred).
try(mssr(matrix(c(1, NA, 3, 4), 2), fwhm = 3)) # non-finite input
#> Error in mssr(matrix(c(1, NA, 3, 4), 2), fwhm = 3) : 
#>   `x` contains NA, NaN or infinite values; MSSR is undefined for them.

    Interactive exploration

    mssr_app() opens the same computations in a Shiny app (it needs the shiny, bslib, jsonlite, callr and digest packages). It shows the input and the structure map on the same input-pixel axes, line profiles, masks measured on the input and the self-test, and offers the results for download. The examples above are available there, and frames can be uploaded as text tables, PNG or TIFF.

    Computation runs in one background job per app session. Cancel stops the owned job, and incomplete results cannot be exported. A previous completed input, settings and mask can be explicitly restored. The run record distinguishes restored results and settings captured at computation from current controls. A session closing or a five-minute limit stops its unfinished job. Development source launches need pkgload; installed-package launches use the exact installed namespace and verify their loaded definitions.

    mssr_app()

    Checking an installation

    mssr_selftest() recomputes the bundled synthetic fixtures. They were produced by the package’s engine definition, so this is a regression check of the installation, not an independent validation:

    st <- mssr_selftest()
st[, c("fixture_id", "max_abs_error", "passed")]
#>                           fixture_id max_abs_error passed
#> 1                       fx01_amp1_o1  5.551115e-16   TRUE
#> 2                fx02_amp1_o1_nonorm  0.000000e+00   TRUE
#> 3                  fx02_amp1_o1_norm  0.000000e+00   TRUE

#> 7                       fx05_amp1_o1  0.000000e+00   TRUE

    Reproducible expert workflow

    Choose FWHM from the acquisition PSF in input-pixel units. Record its source and uncertainty; an image’s dimensions do not establish physical calibration. A measured PSF is preferable to a theoretical one, which describes an ideal system; the recorded PSF can be wider. Under noise a too-small FWHM adds false peaks and a larger one weakens the separation of close sources, so choose the larger plausible value when unsure. Only the kernel half-size in parameters$half_size enters the computation, so compare settings that change it. Fix preprocessing, channel selection, frame boundaries and parameter-selection rules before evaluating outcomes. Cropping changes the neighborhood context and global normalizers, so a cropped reconstruction need not equal a crop of the full-frame result. Background subtraction is a distinct preprocessing decision.

    Start with a low order and compare plausible acquisition-informed settings. Orders above 3 are accepted for compatibility but produce a qualification warning: the expanded independent reference suite found sensitive high-order failures. The bounded passing domain is evidence about the tested scenes, not a guarantee for an arbitrary noisy acquisition. Review broad-object hollowing/splitting, missing dim structures and blank/noise-only fields alongside favorable examples.

    frame <- outer(1:13, 1:17, function(r, c) 0.05 + exp(-((r-7)^2+(c-9)^2)/8))
result <- mssr(frame, fwhm = 3, order = 1)
summary(result)
#> MSSR result summary: intensity_weighted_structure
#>   Grid:        input 13 x 17 -> output 13 x 17 (amp 1, extent grid)
#>   Parameters:  fwhm 3 px, order 1, kernel disk (half-size 2), rounding half_even
#>                intensity weighting TRUE, mesh FALSE
#>   Values:      range 0 to 1.05; zero fraction 0.805; negative fraction 0.000
#>   Diagnostics: defined; 0 undefined order step(s) skipped; 12 offsets
#>   Engine:      mssr_r_rev3, mssrscopR 0.1.0.9004; result schema 1.0.0; evidence numerical_tool_only
#>   Not a quantitative intensity: measure on the original data.
mssr_estimate_resources(dim(frame), fwhm = 3)
#> $input_dim
#> [1] 13 17
#> 
#> $output_dim
#> [1] 13 17
#> 
#> $output_pixels
#> [1] 221
#> 
#> $half_size
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $n_offsets
#> [1] 12
#> 
#> $estimated_work
#> [1] 2652
#> 
#> $estimated_peak_bytes
#> [1] 134272136
#> 
#> $model
#> [1] "whole_frame_buffers_v2"
#> 
#> $hard_limit
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $limitation
#> [1] "Allocation estimate; retained objects and runtime can increase process RSS."

    mssr_validate_result() checks a result’s internal contract. mssr_write_result() and mssr_read_result() use explicit paths, integrity hashes and exact binary values; optional digest and jsonlite are needed for these operations. They do not establish acquisition provenance. Never use reconstructed intensities as calibrated measurements. Original-data measurements under a mask still reflect selection bias: report retained coverage, compare with sensible controls and inspect how small score changes alter the selected population.

    mssr_batch() processes a named list of independent whole frames with one worker. It records failures and cancellations, checks completed results before reuse and retains separate attempts. It checks cancellation between frames. Its memory budget is a conservative estimate; use a separate process-level limit when a hard memory cap is required. It does not implement tiling or infer time, depth, wavelength, specimen identity or physical units from an array.

    Save and replay an analysis

    mssr_settings() validates the result and returns only callable computation settings, including the grid. Passing result$parameters directly is not a replay recipe: it includes a derived kernel half-size and omits the grid. Settings are resolved values, so mesh compensation is recorded as off when amplification is 1. Resource budgets are not retained settings; choose them explicitly when recomputing.

    The example below retains the original synthetic frame and mask context in memory, then reads the exact result from a file. For a durable analysis, keep the original frame in trusted storage and retain its identity, preprocessing, channel/frame selection, acquisition information and mask context alongside it. The .mssr file does not contain those inputs. Here no acquisition calibration is available, and FWHM is a chosen synthetic setting.

    original <- frame
context <- list(
  preprocessing = "none; authored synthetic frame",
  region = outer(seq_len(nrow(original)), seq_len(ncol(original)),
                 function(r, c) r <= 10 & c >= 4),
  fraction = 0.2,
  seed = 23L
)
result <- mssr(original, fwhm = 3, amp = 2, order = 1,
               max_output_pixels = 5e7, max_memory_bytes = 1024^3)
mask <- mssr_mask(result, fraction = context$fraction,
                  region = context$region, seed = context$seed)
measurement <- mean(original[mask])

if (requireNamespace("digest", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".mssr")
  mssr_write_result(result, path)
  restored <- mssr_read_result(path)
  stopifnot(identical(restored$engine$package_version,
                      as.character(packageVersion("mssrscopR"))))
  replay <- do.call(mssr, c(
    list(x = original, max_output_pixels = 5e7, max_memory_bytes = 1024^3),
    mssr_settings(restored)
  ))
  replay_mask <- mssr_mask(replay, fraction = context$fraction,
                           region = context$region, seed = context$seed)
  stopifnot(identical(replay$values, restored$values),
            identical(replay$transform, restored$transform),
            identical(replay_mask, mask),
            identical(mean(original[replay_mask]), measurement))
  unlink(path)
}

    Preserve the package artifact and runtime environment with a durable analysis, for example by retaining sessionInfo() output. The helper refuses results from a different numerical engine and does not migrate historical results. A legacy result schema with the current engine can still supply validated settings. Matching engine and settings is not a promise of identical arithmetic across package versions or environments: verify values and the original-data measurement after replay. The measurement remains subject to mask selection; successful reproduction does not validate the scientific choice of mask.
